en: The Amarakośa, also known as the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana; Section 1:
The First Book, titled the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana, is the Amarakośa.
Invocation:
O wise ones, may that unfathomable ocean of wisdom and compassion, whose virtues are pure and inexhaustible, be served for the sake of prosperity and immortality.
Introduction (1.0.3): Having drawn together other treatises, this instruction on names and genders is here declared complete in its sections, composed in concise and refined verses (1.0.4).
(1.0.5) The technical definitions [are established] mostly by means of differences in form and, in some cases, by association;
(1.0.6) [the gender] should be understood as feminine, masculine, or neuter, though in some instances it is known through specific rules regarding those [terms].

(1.0.7) To express distinctions, neither a copulative compound (*dvandva*), nor a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*), nor a confusion [of genders] has been employed here. (1.0.8) Nor have words of different genders been used for those not explicitly mentioned, except in accordance with the sequence. (1.0.9) In the section on the three genders, the word "in the three" (*triṣu*) is used; however, in the section on pairs, the word "in the two" (*dvayoḥ*) is used.
(1.0.10) The prohibited suffixes *liṅga* are for the purpose of the remainder; however, words beginning with *anta* and *atha* do not precede [the word they modify].
The section on heaven (1.1.11): *svarga*, *avyaya*, *svarga*, *nāka*, *tridiva*, and *tridaśālaya*.
(1.1.12) *suraloka*, *dyu*, and *div*—these two [words] are feminine; *triviṣṭapa* is neuter.
(1.1.13) *amara*, *nirjara*, *deva*, *tridaśa*, *vibudha*, and *sura*;
(1.1.14) *suparvan*, *sumanas*, *tridiveśa*, and *divaukas*.
(1.1.15) The sons of Aditi, the dwellers of heaven, the rows [of gods], the delights of Aditi;
(1.1.16) the Ādityas, the Ṛbhus, the sleepless, the immortal, those whose food is nectar;
(1.1.17) those for whom the sacrificial grass is their mouth, who enjoy the seasons, the gods, the enemies of the Dānavas.
(1.1.18) *Vṛndāraka* and *daivata* are masculine, or *devatā* is feminine.
(1.1.19) The Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Vasus, Tuṣitas, Ābhāsvaras, and Anilas;
(1.1.20) the Mahārājikas, Sādhyas, and Rudras are the deities of the [divine] hosts (*gaṇadevatā*).

(1.1.21) Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras; (1.1.22) Piśācas, Guhyakas, Siddhas, and Bhūtas—these are the divine origins (devayoni); (1.1.23) Asuras, Daityas, Daiteyas, Danujas, Indrāris, and Dānavas.
(1.1.24) The sons of Diti, enemies of the gods, were the former deities, the disciples of Śukra.
(1.1.25) The All-Knowing One, the Sugata, the Buddha, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata;
(1.1.26) the Samantabhadra, the Blessed One, the Conqueror of Māra, the Conqueror of the World, the Jina.

(1.1.27) He who possesses the six superknowledges, the one endowed with the ten powers, the teacher of non-duality, the Guide; (1.1.28) the Lord of Sages, the embodiment of glory, the Teacher, the Sage, he who is Śākyamuni;
(1.1.29) he is the Lion of the Śākyas, Sarvārthasiddha, and Śauddhodani.
(1.1.30) He is Gautama, Arkabandhu, and the son of Māyādevī; (1.1.31) Brahmā, the self-born, the eldest of the gods, Parameṣṭhin, and Pitāmaha;
(1.1.32) Hiraṇyagarbha, Lord of the World, Svayaṃbhū, and the Four-faced One.
(1.1.33) Dhātṛ, Abjayoni, Druhiṇa, Viriñci, Kamalāsana;
(1.1.34) Sraṣṭṛ, Prajāpati, Vedhā, Vidhātṛ, Viśvasṛj, Vidhi;
(1.1.35) Nābhijanman, Aṇḍaja, Pūrva, Nidhana, Kamalodbhava.
(1.1.36) Ever-blissful, the embodiment of passion (*rajas*), Satyaka, whose vehicle is the swan;
(1.1.37) Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṭaraśravas; (1.1.38) Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, Mādhava, Svabhū.
The enemy of the Daityas, the lotus-eyed one, Govinda, he whose banner is Garuḍa;
the one clad in yellow garments, the infallible Acyuta, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Viṣvaksena, Janārdana;
Upendra, the younger brother of Indra, the wielder of the discus, the four-armed one.
(1.1.42) Padmanābha, Madhuripu, Vāsudeva, Trivikrama; (1.1.43) Devakīnandana, Śauri, Śrīpati, Puruṣottama; (1.1.44) Vanamālī, Balidhvaṃsī, Kaṃsārāti, Adhokṣaja.
(1.1.45) Viśvaṃbhara, Kaiṭabhajit, Vidhu, Śrīvatsalāñchana;
(1.1.46) Purāṇapuruṣa, Yajñapuruṣa, Narakāntaka; (1.1.47) Jalaśāyī, Viśvarūpa, Mukunda, Muramardana.
(1.1.48) Vasudeva is his father; he himself is Ānakadundubhi.
(1.1.49) Balabhadra, the slayer of Pralamba, is Baladeva, the elder brother of Acyuta.
(1.1.50) He is Revatīramaṇa, Rāma, Kāmapāla, and Halāyudha.
Nīlāmbara, Rauhineya, Tālāṅka, Musalī, Halī,
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Sīrapāṇi, Kālindībhedana, and Bala; Madana, Manmatha, Māra, Pradyumna, and Mīnaketana.
(1.1.54) Kandarpa, Darpaka, Anaṅga, Kāma, Pañcaśara, Smara; (1.1.55) Śambarāri, Manasija, Kusumeṣu, Ananyaja; (1.1.56) Puṣpadhanvan, Ratipati, Makaradhvaja, Ātmabhū.
The lotus, the aśoka, the mango, the fresh jasmine, and the blue water-lily—these five are the arrows of the Five-Arrowed One. They are:
the intoxicating, the scorching, the withering, and likewise the paralyzing.

(1.1.60) Sammohana and Kāma are proclaimed as the five arrows. (1.1.61) Brahmasū is Viśvaketu, and Aniruddha is the husband of Uṣā. (1.1.62) Lakṣmī is Padmālayā, Padmā, Kamalā, Śrī, and the beloved of Hari.
(1.1.63) Indirā, the mother of the world, Mā, the daughter of the Milky Ocean, Ramā; (1.1.64) Bhārgavī, the progenitor of the world, the maiden of the milk-ocean;
(1.1.65) Śaṅkha, the Pāñcajanya conch of the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Sudarśana discus.
(1.1.66) The Kaumodakī mace, the sword Nandaka, and the Kaustubha jewel;
(1.1.67) the bow Śārṅga belongs to Murāri, and the Śrīvatsa is known as his mark;
(1.1.68) and the horses are Śaivya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka.
(1.1.69) His charioteer is Dāruka, his counselor is Uddhava, and his younger brother is Gada.
(1.1.70) Garuḍa is Garutmān, Tārkṣya, Vainateya, and Khageśvara.
(1.1.71) He is the end of serpents, the chariot of Viṣṇu, Suparṇa, and the devourer of *pannagas*.
(1.1.72) Śambhu, Īśa, Paśupati, Śiva, Śūlin, Maheśvara;
(1.1.73) Īśvara, Śarva, Īśāna, Śaṅkara, Candraśekhara; (1.1.74) Bhūteśa, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Girīśa, Giriśa, Mṛḍa.
(1.1.75) Conqueror of Death, clad in animal skins, wielder of the Pināka bow, Lord of the Pramathas;
(1.1.76) Fierce One, with matted hair, Śrīkaṇṭha, blue-throated, bearer of the skull;
(1.1.77) Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Virūpākṣa, the three-eyed one.
(1.1.78) Kṛśānuretās, Sarvajña, Dhūrjaṭi, Nīlalohita; (1.1.79) Hara, Smarahara, Bharga, Tryambaka, Tripurāntaka;
(1.1.80) Gaṅgādhara, Andhakaripu, Kratudhvaṃsin, Vṛṣadhvaja.
(1.1.81) Vyomakeśa, Bhava, Bhīma, Sthāṇu, Rudra, Umāpati;
(1.1.82) Ahirbudhnya, Aṣṭamūrti, Gajāri, and Mahānata; (1.1.83) His matted hair is called Kaparda; his bow is Pināka, also known as Ajagava.
(1.1.84) The *pramathas* are the attendants (*pāriṣadas*); the Mothers are Brāhmī and the others.
(1.1.85) *Vibhūti*, *bhūti*, and *aiśvarya* consist of the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
(1.1.86) These are: *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *garimā*, and likewise *laghimā*;
(1.1.87) Attainment, the power of irresistible will, lordship, and mastery—these are the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
(1.1.88) Umā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, Kālī, Haimavatī, Īśvarī;
(1.1.89) Śivā, Bhavānī, Rudrāṇī, Śarvāṇī, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
Aparṇā, Pārvatī, Durgā, Mṛḍānī, Caṇḍikā, Ambikā;
Āryā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Girijā, Menakātmajā; Karmamoṭī, Cāmuṇḍā, Carmamuṇḍā, and Carcikā.
Vināyaka, Vighnarāja, the son of the two mothers, and Gaṇādhipa; also Ekadanta, Heramba, Lambodara, and Gajānana; Kārtikeya, Mahāsena, Śarajanman, and Ṣaḍānana.
Skanda is the son of Pārvatī, the leader of the army, born of Agni, and Guha; he is the son of Bahulā, the conqueror of Tāraka, Viśākha, and the one whose vehicle is the peacock;
he is the son of six mothers, the wielder of the spear, Kumāra, and the destroyer of Krauñca.
(1.1.99) Śṛṅgī, Bhṛṅgī, Riṭi, Tuṇḍī, Nandika, and Nandikeśvara;
(1.1.100) Indra, Marutvān, Maghavān, Biḍaujas, and Pākaśāsana;
(1.1.101) Vṛddhaśravas, Sunāsīra, Puruhūta, and Purandara.
(1.1.102) Jiṣṇu, Lekharṣabha, Śakra, Śatamanyu, Divaspati;
(1.1.103) Sutrāman, Gotrabhit, Vajrin, Vāsava, Vṛtrahan, Vṛṣan;
(1.1.104) Bāstoṣpati, Surapati, Balārāti, Śacīpati.
(1.1.105) Jambhabhedin, Harihaya, Svārāṭ, Namucisūdana;
(1.1.106) Saṃkrandana, Duścyavana, Turāṣāṭ, Meghavāhana;
(1.1.107) Ākhaṇḍala, Sahasrākṣa, Ṛbhukṣan. His beloved wife, however, is...
(1.1.108) Pulomajā, Śacī, and Indrāṇī [are names of Indra’s wife]; his city, however, is Amarāvatī.
(1.1.109) His horse is Uccaiḥśravas; his charioteer is Mātali; his grove is Nandana. (1.1.110) His palace is Vaijayanta; Jayanta is the son of Pākaśāsana (Indra).
Airāvata, abhramātaṅga, airāvaṇa, and abhramuvallabha are synonyms for Indra’s elephant.
Hrādinī, vajra, kuliśa, bhidura, and pavi denote the thunderbolt; the latter is not feminine.
Śatakoṭi, svaru, śamba, dambholi, and aśani are terms for the thunderbolt, with the last two being used in both genders.
(1.1.114) A celestial vehicle is called a *vimāna* (not feminine); Nārada and others are the divine sages (*surarṣi*).
(1.1.115) The assembly hall of the gods is *Sudharmā*; nectar is *pīyūṣa*, *amṛta*, and *sudhā*.
(1.1.116) The Mandākinī is the celestial Gaṅgā, the golden river, and the long pool of the gods.
(1.1.117) Meru, Sumeru, Hemādri, Ratnasānu, and Surālaya;
(1.1.118) these five are the celestial trees: Mandāra, Pārijātaka, Santāna, and Kalpavṛkṣa; or [the last] may be Haricandana in the masculine.
(1.1.120) Sanatkumāra is the son of Vidhātṛ; the two physicians of heaven are the sons of the Aśvins.
(1.1.121) They are called Nāsatyas, Aśvins, Dasras, and both are known as Āśvineyas.
(1.1.122) In the feminine gender and in the plural, they are the Apsarases—the celestial courtesans headed by Urvaśī.
(1.1.123) Hāhā, Hūhū, and others such as these are the Gandharvas of the denizens of heaven. (1.1.124) Agni, Vaiśvānara, Vahni, Vītihotra, and Dhanañjaya;
(1.1.125) Kṛpīṭayoni, Jvalana, Jātavedas, and Tanūnapāt.
(1.1.126) Barhis, Śuṣma, Kṛṣṇavartman, Śociṣkeśa, Uparbudha;
(1.1.127) Āśrayāśa, Bṛhadbhānu, Kṛśānu, Pāvaka, Anala; (1.1.128) Rohitāśva, Vāyusakha, Śikhāvān, Āśuśukṣaṇi.
Hiraṇyaretas, Hutabhuj, Dahana, Havyavāhana;
Saptārcis, Damunas, Śukra, Citrabhānu, Vibhāvasu; Śuci, Appitta, Aurva, Vāḍava, and Vaḍavānala.
(1.1.132) *Jvālā*, *kīla*, *arcis*, *hetis*, and *śikhā* are feminine terms for the flame or crest of fire.
(1.1.133) *Sphuliṅga* and *agnikaṇa* are masculine-feminine- neuter (*triṣu*) for a spark; *saṃtāpa* and *saṃjvara* are synonyms for heat.
(1.1.134) *Ulkā* refers to a meteor or a firebrand with flames issuing forth; *bhūti*, *bhasita*, and *bhasman* denote ashes.
(1.1.135) *Kṣāra*, *rakṣā*, and *dāva*—the latter being a forest fire (*dava*);
(1.1.136) *dharmarāja*, *pitṛpati*, *samavartī*, and *paretarāṭ*;
(1.1.137) *kṛtānta*, *yamunābhrātā*, *śamana*, *yamarāṭ*, and *yama*.
(1.1.138) Kāla, Daṇḍadhara, Śrāddhadeva, Vaivasvata, Antaka; (1.1.139) Rākṣasa, Koṇapa, Kravyād, Kravyāda, Asrapa, Āśara; (1.1.140) Rātriñcara, Rātricara, Karbura, and Nikaṣātmaja.
(1.1.141) Yātudhāna, Puṇyajana, Nairṛta, Yātu, and Rakṣas;
(1.1.142) Pracetas, Varuṇa, Pāśin, Lord of aquatic creatures, and Lord of waters; (1.1.143) Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Mātariśvan, and Sadāgati.
(1.1.144) Pṛṣadaśva, Gandhavaha, Gandhavāha, Anila, Āśuga; (1.1.145) Samīra, Māruta, Marut, Jagatprāṇa, Samīraṇa;
(1.1.146) Nabhasvat, Vāta, Pavana, Pavamāna, Prabhañjana.
(1.1.147) A violent wind that causes great trembling is a gale accompanied by rain.
(1.1.148) Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna are the vital breaths (vāyus). (1.1.149) These reside within the body; furthermore, raṃhas, taras, rayas, and syadas denote speed.

(1.1.150) *java*, *śīghra*, *tvarita*, *laghu*, *kṣipra*, *ara*, *druta*; (1.1.151) *satvara*, *capala*, *tūrṇa*, *avilambita*, and *āśu* [denote speed]; (1.1.152) *satata*, *anārata*, *aśrānta*, *saṃtata*, *avirata*, and *aniśam* [denote continuity].

(1.1.153) *nitya*, *anavarata*, and *ajasram* [mean "constantly"]; furthermore, *atiśaya*, *bhara*, (1.1.154) *ativela*, *bhṛśa*, *atyartha*, *atimātra*, *udgāḍha*, and *nirbhara*; (1.1.155) *tīvra*, *ekānta*, *nitānta*, as well as *gāḍha*, *bāḍha*, and *dṛḍha* [all mean "intense" or "excessive"].
(1.1.156) When denoting speed and the like, the word *klība* is neuter; when denoting a quality (*sattva*), it is used in all three genders.
(1.1.157) Kubera is the friend of Tryambaka, the king of the Yakṣas, and the lord of the Guhyakas.
(1.1.158) He is Manuṣyadharman, Dhanada, Rājarāja, and Dhanādhipa.
Vaiśravaṇa is the lord of the Kinnaras, a descendant of Pulastya, and has men as his vehicle;
he is also known as Yakṣa, Ekapiṅga, Ilavila, Śrīda, and Puṇyajaneśvara.
His pleasure garden is Caitraratha, and his son is Nalakūbara.
(1.1.162) Kailāsa is the abode [of Śiva], and Alakā is the city; the Puṣpaka is the celestial vehicle. (1.1.163) A Kinnara is also called a Kiṃpuruṣa; a horse-faced being is a Mayu.
(1.1.164) A treasure is called a nidhi or a śevadhi; the varieties of treasure include the Padma, Śaṅkha, and others.
Mahāpadma, Padma, Śaṅkha, Makara, Kacchapa, Mukunda, Kunda, and Nīla, along with Kharva— these are the nine treasures (nidhis); [the square root of] the sky (vyoma) is the square (varga).
(1.2.167) *dyo*, *div*— these two [words] are feminine; *abhra*, *vyoman*, *puṣkara*, *ambara*,
(1.2.168) *nabhas*, *antarikṣa*, *gagana*, *ananta*, *suravartman*, *kha*,
(1.2.169) *viyat*, *viṣṇupada*, and also *ākāśa* and *vihāyas* are masculine.
(1.2.170) *vihāyas*, *nāka*, and *dyu* may also be used [for the sky].
(1.2.171) *Tārāpatha*, *antarikṣa*, *meghādhvan*, and *mahābila* [are synonyms for the sky].
(1.2.172) *Vihāyas* is masculine when referring to a bird, and both masculine and neuter when referring to the sky.
The group of words for directions (dig-varga):
(1.3.173) The directions are *diśas*, *kakubhas*, *kāṣṭhās*, *āśās*, and *haritas*.
(1.3.174) *Prācī*, *avācī*, and *pratīcī* are the east, south, and west respectively.
(1.3.175) *uttarā* and *udīcī* denote the north; that which pertains to the direction (*diśyam*) occurs in three genders.
(1.3.176) That which arises from the downward direction is *avācīnam*; that which arises from the upward direction is *udīcīnam*, as is *udagbhavam*.
(1.3.177) That which arises from the west is *pratīcīnam*; that which arises from the east is *prācīnam*; these occur in all three genders.
Indra, Vahni, Pitṛpati, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Marut,
Kubera, and Īśa are, in order, the lords of the directions beginning with the East.
[The planets are] Ravi, Śukra, Mahīsūnu, Svarbhānu, Bhānuja, and Vidhu.
Budha and Bṛhaspati, as well as the planets of the quarters;
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda,
Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the directions.
(1.3.184) The female elephants are, in order: Abhramukā, Kapilā, Piṅgalā, Anupamā; (1.3.185) Tāmrakarṇī, Śubhradantī, Aṅganā, and Añjanāvatī.
(1.3.186) The indeclinable *apadiśam* refers to the intermediate direction between two cardinal directions; it is feminine when denoting a *vidiś* (intermediate point).
(1.3.187) *Abhyantara* means the interior or interval; *cakravāla*, however, means a circle.
(1.3.188) *Abhra*, *megha*, *vārivāha*, *stanayitnu*, and *balāhaka*;
(1.3.189) *dhārādhara*, *jaladhara*, *taḍitvān*, *vārida*, and *ambubhṛt* [all mean cloud].
(1.3.190) *ghana*, *jīmūta*, *mudira*, *jalada*, *dhūmayoni*;

(1.3.191) *kādambinī* and *meghamālā* denote a line of clouds; *abhriya* refers to anything produced from a cloud in three genders; (1.3.192) *stanita*, *garjita*, and *rasita* refer to the thundering roar of a cloud.
(1.3.193) Śampā, śatahradā, hrādinī, airāvatī, and kṣaṇaprabhā; (1.3.194) taḍit, saudāminī, vidyut, cañcalā, and capalā are also [names for lightning].
(1.3.195) Sphūrjathu, vajranirghoṣa, meghajyotis, and iraṃmada [are names for thunder].

(1.3.196) *Indrāyudha* is the bow of Śakra; that same [bow] when straight is called *ṛjurohita*. (1.3.197) *Vṛṣṭi* and *varṣa* mean rain; in the cessation of that [rain], *avagrāha* and *avagraha* are synonymous.
(1.3.198) *Āsāra* is the falling of a stream [of rain]; *śīkara* is known to be water droplets.
(1.3.199) *varṣopala* is hail (*karakā*); a day with clouds is a cloudy day (*durdinam*).
(1.3.200) *Antardhā*, *vyavadhā*, and *antardhi*—the latter being masculine—are synonyms for concealment (*apavāraṇa*).
(1.3.201) *Apidhāna*, *tirodhāna*, *apidhāna*, and *ācchādana* are also [synonyms].
Himāṃśu, Candramas, Candra, Indu, Kumudabāndhava,
Vidhu, Sudhāṃśu, Śubhrāṃśu, Oṣadhīśa, Niśāpati, Abja, Jaivātṛka, Soma, Glau, Mṛgāṅka, and Kalānidhi are synonyms for the Moon. (1.3.202–204)
(1.3.205) *dvijarājaḥ*, *śaśadharaḥ*, *nakṣatreśaḥ*, and *kṣapākaraḥ* are synonyms for the moon.

(1.3.206) A *kalā* is the sixteenth part [of the moon]; *bimba* and *maṇḍala* are masculine and neuter, respectively. (1.3.207) *Bhitta*, *śakala*, and *khaṇḍa* denote a split or fragment; *ardha* is masculine when it refers to a portion that is equal [to the whole].
(1.3.208) *Candrikā*, *kaumudī*, and *jyotsnā* denote moonlight; *prasāda* and *prasannatā* denote clarity or serenity.
(1.3.209) *Kalaṅka*, *aṅka*, *lāñchana*, *cihna*, *lakṣma*, and *lakṣaṇa* denote a mark, blemish, or sign.
(1.3.210) *Suṣamā* denotes supreme beauty; *śobhā*, *kānti*, *dyuti*, and *chavi* denote splendor or luster.
(1.3.211) *avaśyāya*, *nīhāra*, *tuṣāra*, *tuhina*, and *himam* [mean frost].
(1.3.212) *prāleya* and *mihikā* mean mist; furthermore, *himānī* means a mass of snow.
(1.3.213) *śīta* refers to the quality [of coldness]; words with similar meanings include *suṣīma*, *śiśira*, and *jaḍa*.
Tuṣāra, śītala, śīta, and hima—these seven are of various genders.
(1.3.215) Dhruva is called Auttānapādi; Agastya is Kumbhasambhava.
(1.3.216) Maitrāvaruṇi is another name for him; Lopāmudrā is his lawful wife.
(1.3.217) *nakṣatra*, *ṛkṣa*, *bha*, *tārā*, *tārakā*, and *uḍu* are synonyms for a star; the last may also be feminine.

(1.3.218) The daughters of Dakṣa (*dākṣāyaṇyaḥ*) refer to the stars beginning with Aśvinī; *aśvayuk* and *aśvinī* are names for the same [star]. (1.3.219) *rādhā* and *viśākhā* are names for the same [star]; *sidhya* and *tiṣya* are names for Puṣya; and *śraviṣṭhā* is used for the same [star].

(1.3.220) The *samā*, *dhaniṣṭhā*, *proṣṭhapadā*, and *bhādrapadā* are feminine. (1.3.221) *Mṛgaśīrṣa* and *mṛgaśiras* [are synonyms]; the latter also refers to *āgrahāyaṇī*. (1.3.222) The *ilvalā* are the stars that reside in the region of its head.
Bṛhaspati is the preceptor of the gods, Gīṣpati, Dhiṣaṇa, and Guru.
Jīva, Āṅgirasa, Vācaspati, and Citraśikhaṇḍija [are also names for him].
Śukra is the preceptor of the Daityas, Kāvya, Uśanas, Bhārgava, and Kavi.
Aṅgāraka, Kuja, Bhauma, Lohitāṅga, and Mahīsuta are names for Mars. Rauhiṇeya, Budha, and Saumya are synonyms for Mercury. Sauri and Śanaiścara are equivalent terms for Saturn.
Tamas, Rāhu, Svarbhānu, Saiṃhikeya, and Vidhuntuda are names for Rāhu.
(1.3.229) The Seven Sages, headed by Marīci and Atri, are the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
(1.3.230) The rising of the zodiacal signs is the *lagna*; these are Aries, Taurus, and so forth.
(1.3.231) Sūra, Sūrya, Aryaman, Āditya, the Twelve-Souled One, and Divākara [are synonyms for the Sun].
(1.3.232) Bhāskara, Ahaskara, Bradhna, Prabhākara, and Vibhākara; (1.3.233) Bhāsvat, Vivasvat, Saptāśva, Haridaśva, and Uṣṇaraśmi;
(1.3.234) Vikartana, Arka, Mārtaṇḍa, Mihira, Aruṇa, and Pūṣan.
(1.3.235) Dyumaṇi, Taraṇi, Mitra, Citrabhānu, Virocana;
(1.3.236) Vibhāvasu, Grahapati, Tviṣāmpati, Aharpati; (1.3.237) Bhānu, Haṃsa, Sahasrāṃśu, Tapana, Savitṛ, Ravi.
(1.3.238) You have lotus-eyes, a mass of splendor, the lord of shadows, and the destroyer of darkness;
(1.3.239) the witness of karma, the eye of the world, the kinsman of the world, whose body is the three Vedas;
(1.3.240) the illuminator, the jewel of the day, a firefly [in comparison], the friend of the world.
(1.3.241) Ina, Bhaga, Bhāmanidhi, Aṃśu, Mālyavān, and Ajinīpati; (1.3.242) Māṭhara, Piṅgala, and Daṇḍa are the attendants at the sides of Caṇḍāṃśu (the Sun).
(1.3.243) Sūrasūta, Aruṇa, Anūru, Kāśyapi, and Garuḍāgraja [are his names].
(1.3.244) *pariveṣa* and *paridhi* refer to the halo around the sun; (1.3.245) *kiraṇa*, *usra*, *mayūkha*, *aṃśu*, *gabhasti*, *ghṛṇi*, and *raśmi*;
(1.3.246) *bhānu*, *kara*, and *marīci* [are synonyms for a ray]; *dīdhiti* is used for both masculine and feminine, while [the following] is feminine.
(1.3.247) *prabhā*, *ruci*, *ruca*, *tviṭ*, *bhās*, *bhā*, *chavi*, *dyuti*, and *dīpti* [are synonyms for light].
(1.3.248) *rociḥ* and *śociḥ* are both neuter; *prakāśaḥ*, *dyotaḥ*, and *ātapaḥ* [are also synonyms for light].
(1.3.249) *Koṣṇam*, *kavoṣṇam*, *mandoṣṇam*, and *kaduṣṇam* [mean "slightly warm"]; these are used in the three genders when referring to that which possesses the quality.
(1.3.250) *Tigma*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *khara* are synonyms for sharpness; likewise, *mṛgatṛṣṇā* and *marīcikā* refer to a mirage.
(1.4.251) *Kāla*, *diṣṭa*, *anehā*, and *samaya* denote time; furthermore, *pakṣati* refers to the first day of a lunar fortnight.

(1.4.252) These two, *pratipad* and *dve*, denote the feminine state; the lunar days beginning with those [names] apply to both genders. (1.4.253) *Ghasra*, *dina*, and *ahar* are masculine, while *divasa* and *vāsara* are neuter. (1.4.254) *Pratyūṣa*, *aharmukha*, *kalya*, *uṣas*, and *pratyuṣas* also [denote the dawn].

(1.4.255) *Vyuṣṭam* and *vibhātam* are two neuter terms; it is held that [the word] *gosarga* is masculine. (1.4.256) *Prabhātam* is also [masculine]; but at the end of the day, *sāyam*, *sandhyā*, and *pitṛprasūḥ* [are feminine].
(1.4.257) *Prāhṇa*, *aparāhṇa*, and *madhyāhna* constitute the three junctions (*trisandhya*); now, *śarvarī* [is feminine for "night"].
(1.4.258) Niśā, niśīthinī, rātri, triyāmā, kṣaṇadā, kṣapā; (1.4.259) vibhāvarī, tamasvinī, rajanī, yāminī, tamī;
(1.4.260) tamisrā, tāmasī—these are synonyms for night. A night endowed with moonlight is called jyautsnī.
(1.4.261) When joined with [an action] worthy of the future or the present, the night is called *pakṣiṇī*.
(1.4.262) *Gaṇarātra* refers to many nights; *pradoṣa* is the beginning of the night. (1.4.263) *Ardharātra* and *niśītha* both mean midnight; *yāma* and *prahara* are synonyms for a watch.

(1.4.264) That junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*) is the interval between the first day (*pratipad*) and the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*). (1.4.265) The two fifteenth days at the ends of the fortnights are both called *pañcadaśī*; the full moon day is *paurṇamāsī* or *paurṇimā*.
(1.4.266) When the moon is deficient by one digit (*kalā*), it is *anumati*; when the moon is full, it is *rākā*.
(1.4.267) Amāvāsyā, amāvasyā, and darśa denote the conjunction of the sun and moon. (1.4.268) When the moon is visible, that day is sinīvālī; when the digits of the moon have vanished, it is kuhū.
(1.4.269) Uparāga and graha refer to an eclipse, occurring when both the moon and the sun are seized by Rāhu.
(1.4.270) *Sopaplava* and *uparakti* are two terms for an eclipse; *agnyutpāta* and *upāhita* are two terms for a portentous fire.
(1.4.271) By a single expression, *puṣpavantau* refers to both the sun and the moon.
(1.4.272) Eighteen *nimeṣas* constitute one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty such *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *kalā*.
(1.4.273) Thirty of those [tatkṣaṇas] are a kṣaṇa; twelve of those are a muhūrta.

(1.4.274) Thirty of those are a day and night (ahorātra); fifteen of those are a fortnight (pakṣa). (1.4.275) The two fortnights, the first and the latter, are the bright and the dark [halves]; both of those together constitute a month (māsa).
Two months each, beginning with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, constitute a season (*ṛtu*); three of these seasons make a solstice (*ayana*).
(1.4.277) Two solstices—the northern and the southern course of the sun—constitute a year (*vatsara*).
(1.4.278) At the time when day and night are equal, that is the equinox (*viṣuvat*), and it is also called *viṣuva*.

The full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) associated with the *puṣpa* constellation is called *pauṣī*; the month in which it occurs is named Pauṣa. The other eleven months, beginning with Māgha, are likewise [named after their respective constellations].
The month of Mārgaśīrṣa is also called Sahā, Mārga, and Āgrahāyaṇika.
In Pauṣa, there are the two months Taiṣa and Sahasya; Tapas refers to Māgha, while Phālguna is called Tapasya. Caitra is known as Caitrika and Madhu;
Vaiśākha is Mādhava and Rādha; Jyeṣṭha is Śukra, and this month is Śuci.

The month of Āṣāḍha is called *nabhāḥ* and *śrāvaṇika*; the month of Śrāvaṇa is likewise [called] *nabhasya*, *prauṣṭhapada*, *bhādra*, and *bhādrapada*. The month of Āśvina is also called *iṣ* and *āśvayuja*; the month of Kārttika is [called] *tuṣāra*.
(1.4.288) Bāhula and Ūrja are names for Kārtika; Hemanta and Śiśira are masculine or neuter.
(1.4.289) Vasanta is the season of flowers and Surabhi; Grīṣma is Ūṣmaka.
(1.4.290) Nidāgha, Uṣṇopagama, Uṣṇa, Ūṣmāgama, and Tapas are synonyms for the hot season.
(1.4.291) *Prāvṛṭ* is feminine; *varṣā* is feminine in the plural; then *śarat* is feminine.
(1.4.292) These six seasons (*ṛtu*) are masculine; [the names] beginning with *mārga* [are used] in pairs in sequence.
(1.4.293) *Saṃvatsara*, *vatsara*, *abda*, *hāyana*, and *samā*—the last being feminine—are synonyms for year (*śarat*).
(1.4.294) A month [of humans] constitutes a day and night of the ancestors (pitr), and a year [of humans] constitutes a day and night of the gods (daivata).
(1.4.295) Two thousand divine yugas constitute a day and night of Brahmā; these two [periods] are the kalpas for men.
(1.4.296) A manvantara, however, consists of seventy-one divine yugas.

*Saṃvarta*, *pralaya*, *kalpa*, *kṣaya*, and *kalpānta* also denote the dissolution [of the world]. (1.4.298) *Paṅka* is not feminine; *pāpmā* (masculine), *pāpa*, *kilbiṣa*, *kalmaṣa*, (1.4.299) *kaluṣa*, *vṛjina*, *ena*, *agha*, *aṃhas*, *durita*, and *duṣkṛta* denote sin or evil.
(1.4.300) *Dharma* is masculine; *puṇya*, *śreyas*, *sukṛta*, and *vṛṣa* [are synonyms for merit].
(1.4.301) *Mud*, *prīti*, *pramada*, *harṣa*, *pramoda*, *āmada*, and *samada*; (1.4.302) *ānandathu*, *ānanda*, *śarma*, *śāta*, and *sukha* [are synonyms for joy].

(1.4.303) *śvaḥśreyasam*, *śivam*, *bhadram*, *kalyāṇam*, *maṅgalam*, *śubham*; (1.4.304) *bhāvukam*, *bhavikam*, *bhavyam*, *kuśalam*, *kṣemam*—these are neuter; (1.4.305) *śastam* is also [neuter]; furthermore, when used as a substance (*dravya*), they may take all three genders (*triṣu*), such as *pāpam*, *puṇyam*, *sukham*, and so forth.

(1.4.306) *matallikā*, *macarcikā*, *prakāṇḍam*, *udghatal-lajau*—these are words denoting excellence. (1.4.307) *ayaḥ* is that which brings auspiciousness. (1.4.308) *daivam*, *diṣṭam*, *bhāgadheyam*, *bhāgyam*, *niyatiḥ*, and *vidhiḥ*—the last being feminine—are synonyms for destiny.
(1.4.309) *Hetu*, *kāraṇa*, and *bīja* mean cause; *nidāna* means the primary or original cause.
(1.4.310) *Kṣetrajña*, *ātman*, and *puruṣa* denote the self; *pradhāna* and *prakṛti* are feminine terms for primordial nature.
(1.4.311) *Viśeṣa* refers to temporal states; the *guṇas* are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
(1.4.312) *Janu*, *janana*, and *janman* mean birth; *janu*, *utpatti*, and *udbhava* mean origination.
(1.4.313) A living being (*prāṇin*), however, is conscious (*cetana*), born (*janmin*), a creature (*jantu*), one who is to be born (*janya*), and embodied (*śarīrin*).
(1.4.314) *Jāti* and *jāta* refer to the universal (*sāmānya*); *vyakti*, on the other hand, is individuality (*pṛthagātmatā*).
(1.4.315) *Citta*, *cetas*, *hṛdaya*, *svānta*, *hṛd*, *mānasa*, and *manas* are synonyms for the mind (*dhīvarga*).
(1.5.316) *Buddhi*, *manīṣā*, *dhiṣaṇā*, *dhī*, *prajñā*, *śemuṣī*, and *mati* [are synonyms for intelligence].
(1.5.317) *prekṣā*, *upalabdhi*, *cit*, *saṃvit*, *pratipad*, *jñapti*, and *cetanā*;
(1.5.318) *dhī* is that which possesses retention (*dhāraṇā*); *medhā* is the faculty of memory; *saṃkalpa* is mental action (*mānasaṃ karma*);
(1.5.319) as well as *avadhāna*, *samādhāna*, and likewise *praṇidhāna*.
(1.5.320) Mental application (*manaskāra*) is called the expansion of the mind (*cittābhoga*), reflection (*carcā*), enumeration (*saṃkhyā*), investigation (*vicāraṇā*),

deliberation (*vimarśa*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and latent impression (*vāsanā*). (1.5.321–322) Supplementation (*adhyāhāra*), reasoning (*tarka*), conjecture (*ūha*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are called uncertainty (*saṃśaya*).
(1.5.323) Furthermore, *sandeha* and *dvāpara* are synonyms; likewise, *nirṇaya* and *niścaya*.
(1.5.324) *Mithyādṛṣṭi* and *nāstikatā* denote atheism; *vyāpāda* is the thought of malice.
(1.5.325) *Siddhānta* and *rāddhānta* are synonymous; *bhrānti*, *mithyāmati*, and *bhrama* denote error.
(1.5.326) *Saṃvit*, *āgūḥ*, *pratijñāna*, *niyama*, *āśrava*, and *saṃśrava*; (1.5.327) *aṅgīkāra*, *abhyupagama*, *pratiśrava*, and *samādhi* [are synonyms for a promise].
(1.5.328) Wisdom regarding liberation is *jñāna*; elsewhere, it is *vijñāna*, [referring to] arts and sciences.
(1.5.329) Liberation (*mukti*), absolute isolation (*kaivalya*), extinction (*nirvāṇa*), the highest good (*śreyas*), the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and the deathless (*amṛta*);
(1.5.330) release (*mokṣa*) and emancipation (*apavarga*). Furthermore, ignorance (*ajñāna*), nescience (*avidyā*), and the conceit of "I" (*ahaṃmati*) are feminine [nouns].
(1.5.331) Form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), smell (*gandha*), taste (*rasa*), and touch (*sparśa*)—these are the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*).
(1.5.332) The objects of the senses (*gocara*) are the sense-objects, while *hṛṣīka* refers to the sense-faculty as the subject of the object.
(1.5.333) The organs of action (*karmendriya*), however, are the anus and so forth; the organs of cognition (*dhīndriya*) are the mind, the eyes, and so forth.
(1.5.334) *Tuvara* is astringent (*kaṣāya*), which is not feminine; [the other tastes are] sweet, salty, and pungent.
(1.5.335) *tikta* and *amla* are masculine when denoting tastes; these six [tastes] are used in the three genders when referring to things possessing them.
(1.5.336) *Parimala* refers to a fragrance produced by crushing that captivates the minds of people.
(1.5.337) *Āmoda* is that same fragrance which is exceedingly pervasive; it may take any gender up until the mention of its qualities (*guṇa*).
(1.5.338) *Samākarṣī* is that which draws [the scent] toward oneself; *nirhārī* is that which carries it away. *Surabhi* is that which satisfies the sense of smell.
(1.5.339) *Iṣṭagandha* and *sugandhi* denote a pleasant fragrance; *āmodī* is that which perfumes the mouth.
(1.5.340) *Pūtigandha* and *durgandha* denote a foul odor; *visra* is that which has the smell of raw meat.

(1.5.341) *śukla*, *śubhra*, *śuci*, *śveta*, *viśada*, *śyeta*, and *pāṇḍara* [mean white]; (1.5.342) *avadāta*, *sita*, *gaura*, *avalakṣa*, *dhavala*, and *arjuna* [also mean white]; (1.5.343) *hariṇa* and *pāṇḍura* mean pale-white; while *pāṇḍu* means slightly pale, and *dhūsara* means greyish-white.

(1.5.344) *kṛṣṇa* (black), *nīla*, *asita*, *śyāma*, *kāla*, *śyāmala*, and *mecaka*; (1.5.345) *pīta* (yellow), *gaura* (fair/white), *haridrābha* (turmeric-colored); *palāśa*, *harita*, and *harit* (green); (1.5.346) *lohita*, *rohita*, and *rakta* (red); *śoṇa* (crimson), having the luster of a red lotus (*kokanada*).
(1.5.347) That which has an unmanifest redness is *aruṇa*; that which is white-red is *pāṭala*.
(1.5.348) *Śyāva* is brownish; *kapiśa* is tawny; *dhūmra* and *dhūmala* are dark red; (1.5.349) *kaḍāra*, *kapila*, *piṅga*, *piśaṅga*, *kadru*, and *piṅgala* are [all] reddish-brown.
(1.5.350) *Citra*, *kirmīra*, *kalmāṣa*, *śabala*, and *etā* denote variegated colors;

(1.5.351) words such as *śukla* and others, when referring to a quality (*guṇa*), are masculine, but when they refer to that which possesses the quality (*guṇin*), they take the gender of the object. This concludes the section on groups of words.
(1.6.352) *Brāhmī*, *bhāratī*, *bhāṣā*, *gīḥ*, *vāk*, *vāṇī*, and *sarasvatī* are synonyms for speech.
(1.6.353) *Vyāhāra*, *ukti*, *lapitam*, *bhāṣitam*, *vacanam*, and *vacaḥ* are synonyms for spoken words.
(1.6.354) *Apabhraṃśa* is a corrupt word (*apaśabda*); however, in technical treatises (*śāstra*), the term *śabda* refers to that which is expressive (*vācaka*).

(1.6.355) A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of verbal and nominal endings, or it is an action (*kriyā*) connected with its factors (*kāraka*). (1.6.356) *Śruti* is feminine; it means the Veda, the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), and the triple Veda (*trayī*). Dharma, however, is the injunction (*vidhi*) thereof.
(1.6.357) Among the feminine genders, there are the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *yajus*; thus the Vedas are three, and that triad is the *trayī*.
(1.6.358) Regarding the Vedic injunction beginning with "śikṣā" and so forth, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are such that the syllable *oṃ* and the *praṇava* are identical.
(1.6.359) *Itihāsa* refers to past events; the three accents are the *udātta* and the others.
(1.6.360) *Ānvīkṣikī* is logic (*tarka-vidyā*), while *daṇḍanīti* is the science of statecraft (*artha-śāstra*).
(1.6.361) An *ākhyāyikā* is a narrative based on events actually experienced; a *purāṇa* possesses five characteristics.
(1.6.362) A *kathā* is a literary composition involving invention; a *pravahlikā* is a riddle.
(1.6.363) A *smṛti*, however, is a compendium of dharma; a *samāhṛti* is a collection.
(1.6.364) *Samasyā* refers to the meaning of a compound; *kiṃvadantī* and *janaśruti* mean public rumor.
(1.6.365) *Vārtā*, *pravṛtti*, *vṛttānta*, and *udanta* denote news or an account.
Furthermore, (1.6.366) *āhvaya*, *ākhyā*, *āhve*, *abhidhāna*, *nāmadheya*, and *nāma* all signify a name.
(1.6.367) *Hūti* is calling out or summoning; *saṃhūti* is that performed by many.
(1.6.368) *Vivāda* is legal dispute or litigation; *upanyāsa*, however, is the opening of speech.
(1.6.369) *Upoddhāta* is an introductory statement; *śapana* and *śapatha* (masculine) mean an oath.
(1.6.370) *Praśna*, *anuyoga*, and *pṛcchā* mean "question"; *prativākya* and *uttara* are equivalent terms for "reply.
(1.6.371) *Mithyābhiyoga*, *abhyākhyāna*, and *mithyābhiśaṃsana* mean "false accusation. (1.6.372) *Abhiśāpa* means "imprecation"; *praṇāda* refers to a sound born of passion.
(1.6.373) *Yaśas*, *kīrti*, and *samajñā* mean fame; *stava*, *stotra*, *stuti*, and *nuti* mean praise.
(1.6.374) *Āmreḍitam* is that which is spoken twice or thrice; *ghoṣaṇā* is a loud proclamation (*uccairghuṣṭam*).
(1.6.375) *Kāku* is a feminine noun denoting a modification of the voice caused by grief, fear, and the like.
(1.6.376) *Avarṇa*, *ākṣepa*, *nirvāda*, *parīvāda*, and *apavāda* are synonyms for censure.
(1.6.377) *Upakrośa*, *jugupsā*, *kutsā*, and *nindā* refer to reproach.
(1.6.378) *Pāruṣya* and *ativāda* denote harshness, while *bhartsana* is speech intended to cause harm.
(1.6.379) That which is a reproachful censure is *paribhāṣaṇa*.
(1.6.380) In that context, *ākṣāraṇā* is that which is an insult regarding sexual intercourse.
(1.6.381) *Ābhāṣaṇa* is conversation; *pralāpa* is meaningless speech.
(1.6.382) *Anulāpa* is speaking repeatedly; *vilāpa* is lamentation.
(1.6.383) *Vipralāpa* is contradictory speech; *saṃlāpa* is conversation between two people.
(1.6.384) *Supralāpa* is eloquent speech; *apalāpa*, however, is concealment.
(1.6.385) *Codya*, *ākṣepa*, and *abhiyoga* mean challenge; *śāpa* and *ākrośa* mean cursing; *dureṣaṇā* means seeking to harm from afar.
(1.6.386) *Cāṭu* and *caṭu* are not feminine; they denote praise or flattery, specifically false boasting out of affection.
(1.6.387) *Sandeśavāk* and *vācika* refer to a verbal message; the subsequent terms [from this point] apply to all three genders.
(1.6.388) Ruśatī speech is that which is inauspicious; kalyā, however, is of an auspicious nature.
(1.6.389) [Speech that is] exceedingly sweet, conciliatory, agreeable, and heart-pleasing;
(1.6.390) harsh, rough, vulgar, and indecent; and pleasant yet truthful (*sūnṛta*).
Furthermore, that which is confused, afflicted, or mutually contradictory;
that in which syllables and words are dropped, or which is swallowed up, discarded, or uttered too hastily; that which is mumbled, accompanied by spitting, or incoherent—such speech is meaningless.
(1.6.394) That which is without syllables (*anakṣara*) is inexpressible (*avācya*); however, that which is struck down (*āhata*) has a false meaning (*mṛṣārthaka*).
(1.6.395) *Solluṭhana* is sarcastic speech; *sotprāsa* is derisive; *maṇita* is the cooing of sexual pleasure.
(1.6.396) *Śrāvya* is pleasant to hear; *hṛdya* is heart-pleasing; *manohāri* is captivating; *vispaṣṭa* is clearly articulated; *prakaṭodita* is openly expressed.

(1.6.397) Now, *mliṣṭam* means indistinct; *vitatham*, however, means false speech. (1.6.398) *Satyam*, *tathyam*, *ṛtam*, and *samyak*—these [four] apply to that which possesses those qualities in all three genders.
(1.6.399) *Śabda*, *nināda*, *ninada*, *dhvani*, *dhvāna*, *rava*, and *svana* [are synonyms for sound].
(1.6.400) *svāna*, *nirghoṣa*, *nirhrāda*, *nāda*, *nisvāna*, and *nisvana*;
(1.6.401) *ārava*, *rāva*, *saṃrāva*, and *virāva* [denote sound]; then *marmara* (1.6.402) refers to the rustling of garments and leaves, while *śiñjita* refers to the tinkling of ornaments.

(1.6.403) *nikvāṇaḥ*, *nikvaṇaḥ*, *kvāṇaḥ*, *kvaṇaḥ*, and also *kvaṇanam*—these denote the sound of a lute (*vīṇā*). (1.6.404) With prefixes such as *pra-*, there are forms like *prakvāṇa* and *prakvaṇa*. (1.6.405) *Kolāhalaḥ* and *kalakalaḥ* denote a tumultuous noise, while *vāśitam* is the cry of birds or beasts.
(1.6.406) *Strī* refers to a woman; *pratiśrut* and *pratidhvāna* mean an echo; *gītam* and *gānam* are synonymous, meaning song. This concludes the section on drama (1.7.407).
*Niṣāda*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *dhaivata* [are the seven notes].
(1.7.408) And the fifth; thus these seven notes arise from the strings and the throat.

(1.7.409) *Kākalī* refers to a subtle, indistinct sound; *kala* refers to a sweet yet unclear tone. (1.7.410) *Kala* [also denotes] a low (*mandra*) and deep sound, while *tāra* denotes one that is very high; these three [terms] apply to all three [registers].
(1.7.411) The twenty-two-fold sound situated in the middle of men’s chests is *mandra*; (1.7.412) that which is situated in the middle of the throat is *tāra*, and it is sung in the head.
(1.7.413) That which possesses a corresponding rhythm (*laya*) is *ekatāla*; the lute, however, is called *vallakī*.
(1.7.414) That which has three or five strings is a *vīṇā*, while one with seven strings is a *parivādinī*.
(1.7.415) Stringed instruments such as the *vīṇā* are called *tata*; percussion instruments such as the *muraja* drum are called *ānaddha*.
(1.7.416) Wind instruments such as the flute are called *suṣira*, and cymbals made of bell-metal and the like are called *ghana*.

(1.7.417) This musical instrument is of four kinds, known by the names *vāditra* and *ātodya*. (1.7.418–419) The *mṛdaṅga* and *muraja* are varieties; there are three types of the *āṅkya*, *āliṅgya*, and *ūrdhvaka*. The *yaśaḥpaṭaha* and *ḍhakkā* are also types; the *bherī* is feminine, while the *dundubhi* is masculine.
(1.7.420) *Ānaka* is a synonym for *paṭaha* (kettledrum); it is not feminine. *Koṇa* refers to the plectrum used for playing the *vīṇā* and other instruments.

(1.7.421) *Pravāla* is the neck (*daṇḍa*) of the *vīṇā*. *Kakubha*, however, is the hollow cavity (*prasevaka*). (1.7.422) *Kolambaka* is the body (*kāya*) of the instrument; *upanāha* is its fastening or binding.
The various types of musical instruments are the *ḍamaru*, *maḍḍu*, *ḍiṇḍima*, and *jharjhara*; the *mardala*, *paṇava*, and others as well. The terms *nartakī* and *lāsikā* are synonymous.
*Vilambita*, *druta*, and *madhya* refer respectively to slow, fast, and medium tempo; while *tattva*, *ogha*, and *ghana* denote the gradual progression [of the beat].
(1.7.426) *Tāla* is the measure of the duration of time; *laya* is the evenness [of tempo], and it is not feminine. (1.7.427) *Tāṇḍava*, *naṭana*, *nāṭya*, *lāsya*, and *nṛtya* are terms for dancing.
(1.7.428) *Tauryatrika* consists of dance, song, and instrumental music; these three together constitute *nāṭya*.
(1.7.429) *Bhrakuṃsa*, *bhrukuṃsa*, and *bhrūkuṃsa* refer to a dancer;
(1.7.430) in dramatic terminology, a man wearing female attire is called a *gaṇikāñjukā*;
(1.7.431) *āvutta* is the husband of one’s sister, *bhāva* refers to a learned man, and *āvuka* is [a term for] a father.
(1.7.432) *Janaka* and *yuvarāja* refer to a crown prince; *kumāra* and *bhartṛdāraka* also denote a prince.
(1.7.433) A king is called *rājā*, *bhaṭṭāraka*, or *deva*; his daughter is *bhartṛdārikā*.
(1.7.434) The term *devī* applies to one who has been consecrated, while for others it is *bhaṭṭinī*.
(1.7.435) *Abrahmaṇyam* is used when speaking of one who should not be killed; *rāṣṭriya* refers to a king's brother-in-law.
(1.7.436) *Ambā* is a mother; furthermore, *bālā* means a young woman; *vāsū* is a wife; and *ārya* is *māriṣa*.
(1.7.437) *Attikā* is an elder sister; *niṣṭhā* and *nirvahaṇa* are synonymous.
(1.7.438) *Haṇḍe*, *hañje*, and *halā* are used in addressing; [the first two] for a low-born woman, [the last] for a female servant or a friend.
(1.7.439) *Aṅgahāra* and *aṅgavikṣepa* are synonyms; *vyañjaka* and *abhinaya* are also synonymous.
(1.7.440) Those performed through *aṅga* and *sattva* are respectively called *āṅgika* and *sāttvika*; these two terms apply to all three genders.

(1.7.441) The erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the marvelous, the comic, the terrible, (1.7.442) the loathsome, and the furious are the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*). The erotic is pure and radiant;
(1.7.443) the heroic increases enthusiasm; compassion, pity, and tenderness constitute the pathetic.

(1.7.444) *Kṛpā*, *dayā*, and *anukampā* are synonyms for compassion; *anukrośa* is also used. Furthermore, *hasa*, *hāsa*, and *hāsya* denote laughter. (1.7.445–446) *Bībhatsa* and *vikṛta*—this pair of terms—is used in three genders [to describe the loathsome]. Next, *vismaya*, *adbhuta*, *āścarya*, and *citram* denote wonder. Then, *bhairava*...
*dāruṇa*, *bhīṣaṇa*, *bhīṣma*, *ghora*, *bhīma*,
*bhayānaka*, *bhayaṅkara*, *pratibhaya*, *raudra*, and *ugra*— these ten are used in three genders.
*Dara*, *trāsa*, *bhīti*, *bhī*, *sādhvasa*, and *bhaya* [are synonyms for fear].
(1.7.450) A mental modification is *bhāva*; an *anubhāva* is that which makes [the] *bhāva* known. (1.7.451) *Garva*, *abhimāna*, and *ahaṅkāra* are synonyms; *māna* is the inflation of the mind.
(1.7.452) *Darpa*, *avaloka*, *avaṣṭambha*, *cittodreka*, *smaya*, and *mada* are synonyms for pride.
(1.7.453) Disrespect, contempt, humiliation, and disparagement;
(1.7.454) derision, insult, disdain, and neglect;
(1.7.455) bashfulness, shame, modesty, and embarrassment—this [latter] is *apatrapā* when it arises from another.
(1.7.456) *Kṣānti* is endurance; *abhidhyā*, however, is longing for another's property. (1.7.457) *Akṣānti* is intolerance; *īrṣyā* and *asūyā* are the attribution of faults even to virtues.
(1.7.458) *Vaira*, *virodha*, and *vidveṣa* mean enmity; *manyu* and *śoka* mean grief, with *śuc* used in the feminine.
(1.7.459) *Paścāttāpa*, *anutāpa*, and also *vipratīsāra* denote remorse.
(1.7.460) *Kopa*, *krodha*, *amarṣa*, *roṣa*, *pratigha*, *ruṭ*, and *kṛdh*—the last two are feminine—denote anger. (1.7.461) *Śīla* refers to virtuous conduct; *unmāda* is mental derangement.
(1.7.462) *Premā*, *nā* (*premā*), *priyatā*, and *hārda* mean affection; *premasneha* means love or tenderness; *dohada* means longing.
(1.7.463) *Icchā*, *kāṅkṣā*, *spṛhā*, *īhā*, *tṛṭ*, *vāñchā*, *lipsā*, and *manoratha* mean desire.
(1.7.464) *Kāma*, *abhilāṣa*, and *tarṣa* also mean desire; when excessive, it is called *lālasā*, which applies to both genders.
(1.7.465) *Upādhi* is a limiting condition; *ādhi* is mental anguish in a man.
(1.7.466) *Cintā*, *smṛti*, and *ādhyāna* mean reflection or recollection; *utkaṇṭhā* and *utkalikā* are synonyms for longing.
(1.7.467) *Utsāha* and *adhyavasāya* mean perseverance; that which possesses superior power is *vīrya* (heroism).
(1.7.468) *Kapaṭa* is not feminine; *vyāja*, *dambha*, *upadhi*, *chadma*, and *kaitava* denote deceit.
(1.7.469) *Kusṛti*, *nikṛti*, and *śāṭhya* denote dishonesty; *pramāda* and *anavadhānatā* denote negligence.
(1.7.470) *Kautūhala*, *kautuka*, *kutuka*, and *kutūhala* denote curiosity.
(1.7.471–473) In women, *vilāsa*, *bibboka*, *vibhrama*, *lalita*, as well as *helā* and *līlā*— these are the *hāvas*, actions born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-bhāva*).
Also included are *drava*, *kelī*, *parīhāsa*, *krīḍā*, *līlā*, and *narman*.
(1.7.474) *Vyāja*, *apadeśa*, and *lakṣya* mean pretext; *krīḍā*, *khelā*, and *kūrdana* mean play.
(1.7.475) *Gharma* and *nidāgha* mean heat; *sveda* means perspiration; *pralaya* is the state of lost activity.
(1.7.476) *Avahitthā* is the concealment of one's outward appearance; *saṃvega* and *saṃbhrama* are synonyms for agitation.
(1.7.477) A laugh accompanied by a slight snort is *ācchuritaka*; that same laugh with a touch of sarcasm is *smita*. (1.7.478) A moderate laugh is *vihasita*; horripilation is *romaharṣaṇa*.
(1.7.479) *Krandita*, *rudita*, and *kruṣṭa* mean weeping; *jṛmbhā* and *jṛmbhaṇa* refer to yawning, used in three genders.

(1.7.480) *Vipralambha* means deception; *riṅgaṇa* and *skhalana* are synonyms for stumbling. (1.7.481) *Nidrā*, *śayana*, *svāpa*, *svapna*, and also *saṃveśa* denote sleep. (1.7.482) *Tandrī* and *pramīlā* mean drowsiness; *bhrakuṭi*, *bhrukuṭi*, and *bhrūkuṭi* are feminine terms for a frown.
(1.7.483) There may be lack of vision in an unamiable eye; these two, however, are *saṃsiddhi* and *prakṛti*.
(1.7.484) *Svarūpa*, *svabhāva*, and *nisarga*; then *vepathu*, (1.7.485) *kampa*, *kṣaṇa*, *uddharṣa*, *maha*, *uddhava*, and *utsava*.
The section on the subterranean world and serpents:
(1.8.486) Adhobhuvana, pātāla, balisadma, and rasātala denote the subterranean realm.
(1.8.487) Nāgaloka, kuhara, suṣira, vivara, and bila denote a cavity or hole.

(1.8.488) *chidra*, *nirvyathana*, *roka*, *randhra*, *śvabhra*, *vapā*, and *suṣi* denote a hole or cavity. (1.8.489) *Garta* and *avaṭa* refer to a pit or hole in the ground; *suṣira* refers to anything that has a cavity and is used in three genders. (1.8.490) *Andhakāra*, *dhvānta*, *tamisra*, *timira*, and *tamas* denote darkness (the latter being neuter).
(1.8.491) In dense darkness, it is *andhatamasam*; when that darkness has diminished, it is *avatasam* darkness.
(1.8.492) The serpents, the sons of Kadrū, are called *viṣvaksaṃtamasam*.

Their lord is Śeṣa, also known as Ananta; Vāsuki is the king of snakes, while Gonasa is another. (1.8.493) [Note: The provided text contains a numbering error; 1.8.493 should correspond to the final line. 1.8.493: Vāsuki is the king of snakes, while Gonasa is another.
*Tilitsa* refers to the boa constrictor; both *śayu* and *vāhasa* also denote it. *Alagarda* and *jalavyāla* are synonyms for the water-snake. *Rājila* and *duṇḍubha* are equivalent.
*Māludhāna* and *mātulāhi* refer to the hooded snake. *Nirmukta* and *muktakañcuka* mean one that has cast off its skin.
(1.8.497) Sarpa, pṛdāku, bhujaga, bhujaṅga, ahi, and bhujaṅgama;
(1.8.498) āśīviṣa, viṣadhara, cakrī, vyāla, and sarīsṛpa;
(1.8.499) kuṇḍalī, gūḍhapāt, cakṣuḥśravas, kākodara, and phaṇin are synonyms for a serpent.
The *darvīkara*, the *dīrghapṛṣṭha*, the *dandaśūka*, and the *bileśaya*;
the *uraga*, the *pannaga*, the *bhogin*, the *jihmaga*, and the *pavanāśana*;
the *lelihāna*, the *dvirasana*, the *gokarṇa*, and likewise the *kañcukī*.
(1.8.503) *Kumbhīnasa*, *phaṇadhara*, *hari*, and *bhogadhara* [are synonyms for a snake].

(1.8.504) The body of a snake is called *bhoga*; its fang is called *āśī*. (1.8.505) The word *āheya* (belonging to a snake) applies in three genders to poison, bones, and so forth; however, *phaṇā* (hood) is used in two genders (*strī* and *napuṃsaka*) when referring to the hood itself.
(1.8.506) *Kañcuka* and *nirmoka* are synonyms for the slough of a snake; *kṣveḍa*, *garala*, and *viṣa* denote poison.
(1.8.507) *Kākolaka*, *kālakūṭa*, and *halāhala* are both masculine and neuter.
(1.8.508) *Saurāṣṭrika*, *śauklikeya*, *brahmaputra*, and *pradīpana* [are names of specific poisons].
(1.8.509) Dārada and Vatsanābha—these are the nine varieties of poison.
(1.8.510) A physician of poisons, a snake-charmer, a snake-catcher, and a snake-handler; [this concludes] the section on hells.
(1.9.511) *Nāraka*, *naraka*, *niraya*, and *durgati* are synonyms for hell; the latter is feminine.
(1.9.512) Its specific divisions are Tapana, Avīci, Mahāraurava, Raurava, (1.9.513) Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, and so forth. The inhabitants of these hells are called *nārakas*.
(1.9.514) The Vaitaraṇī river is for the *pretas*; misfortune, however, is Nirṛti.
(1.9.515) *Viṣṭi* is forced labor; *kāraṇā*, on the other hand, is torment, which is intense pain.
(1.9.516) Oppression, affliction, anguish, and suffering are synonyms; that which arises from childbirth is *āmanasya*.
(1.9.517) *Kaṣṭa*, *kṛcchra*, and *ābhīla* are synonyms for difficulty; when these refer to a specific object, they function as adjectives.
[The following is] the section on water: (1.10.518) *Samudra*, *abdhi*, *akūpāra*, *pārāvāra*, and *saritpati* [are synonyms for the ocean].
Udanvān, udadhi, sindhu, sarasvān, sāgara, and arṇava; (1.10.520) ratnākara, jalanidhi, yādaḥpati, and apāmpati;
(1.10.521) its specific varieties include the Kṣīroda (the milk ocean), the Lavaṇoda (the salt ocean), and others.
The word *āpaḥ* is feminine and plural; [its synonyms are] *vār*, *vāri*, *salila*, *kamala*, *jala*, *payaḥ*,
*kīlāla*, *amṛta*, *jīvana*, *bhuvana*, *vana*, *kabandha*, *udaka*, *pāthaḥ*, *puṣkara*, and *sarvatomukha*.

Ambhas, arṇas, toya, pānīya, nīra, kṣīra, ambu, śambaram, meghapuṣpa, and ghanarasa are synonyms for water; these three [last] terms may also be used in the masculine. Two words—āpya and ammaya—are used in all three genders. Bhaṅga, taraṅga, ūrmi, and vīci denote a wave; while ūrmi may also be feminine.
(1.10.528) Great waves are called *ullola* and *kallola*; a whirlpool is the swirling of waters (*āvarta*).
(1.10.529) *Pṛṣanti*, *bindu*, and *pṛṣata* are masculine; *vipruṣ* is feminine for a drop.
(1.10.530) *Cakrāṇi* and *puṭabhedāḥ* refer to eddies, as do *bhramāḥ* and *jalanirgamāḥ*.
(1.10.531) *Kūla*, *rodhas*, *tīra*, *pratīra*, and *taṭa* denote the bank; these three [terms] apply to all three genders.

(1.10.532) *Pāra* and *avāra* refer respectively to the further and nearer banks; *pātra* is the space between them. (1.10.533) *Dvīpa* and *antarīpa*—the latter not feminine—denote that which is a bank situated within the water.
That which arises from water is a *pulina* (sandbank); it is also called *saikata*, meaning consisting of sand (*sikatā*).
*Niṣadvara*, *jambāla*, and *paṅka* denote mud; *śāda* and *kardama* are also used for mud, with *śāda* not being feminine.
*Jalocchvāsāḥ* refers to overflow channels; *kūpakāḥ* are small pits or depressions.
The word *nāvya* has three genders when it means "crossable by boat"; in the feminine, it refers to a boat, as in *naus*, *taraṇi*, and *tari*.
*Uḍupa*, *plava*, and *kola* denote a small boat; *srotas* is the natural flow of water.
*Astaras* is the fare for crossing; *droṇī* is a wooden trough that carries water.
(1.10.540) A sea-faring merchant is a *sāṃyātrika*; a helmsman is a *karṇadhāra* or *nāvika*.
(1.10.541) Those who steer are *niyāmaka*s; a boat-pole is a *kūpaka* or *guṇavṛkṣaka*.
(1.10.542) A boat-oar is a *kṣepaṇī*, while a paddle is an *aritra* or *kenipātaka*.

*Abhri* (feminine) is a wooden spade; *sekapātra* and *secanam* refer to a vessel for pouring water. *Ardhanāvam* (neuter) means half of a boat; *atināvaḥ* and *atinu* (masculine/feminine/neuter) mean having passed beyond a boat. [The following] three terms apply to water: *prasannaḥ* and *acchaḥ* (both masculine) mean clear; *kaluṣaḥ* and *āvilah* mean turbid or unclean.

(1.10.546) *Nimna* means deep; *gambhīra* means profound; *uttāna* is its opposite. (1.10.547) *Agādha* refers to that which does not touch the bottom. *Kaivarta*, *dāśa*, and *dhīvara* denote a fisherman. (1.10.548) *Ānāya* and *jāla* (masculine) mean a net; *śaṇasūtra* and *pavitraka* refer to a cord made of hemp.
A fish-basket is called *kuveṇī*; a fish-hook is *baḍiśa*. A broad-scaled fish is a *jhaṣa*, a *matsya*, a *mīna*, a *vaisāriṇa*, or an *aṇḍaja*.
It is also a *visāra* or a *śakulī*; furthermore, a small *śakula* is a *gaḍaka*.

The *sahasradaṃṣṭra*, *pāṭhīna*, *ulūpī*, and *śiśuka* are synonyms [for types of fish]. The *nalamīna* and *cilicima* are also similar. The *proṣṭhī* and *śapharī* refer to the same species in both genders.
A swarm of small-egg fish is called *potādhāna*. Furthermore, *jhaṣāḥ* refers to large fish.
The rohita, madgura, śāla, rājīva, śakula, and timi; as well as the timiṅgila and others—these are the aquatic creatures (yādāṃsi), the beings born in water.
Their varieties include the śiśumāra, udra, śaṅku, makara, and so forth.
(1.10.558) *Kulīra* and *karkaṭaka* mean crab; *kūrma*, *kamaṭha*, and *kacchapa* mean tortoise.

(1.10.559) *Grāha* and *avahāra* mean crocodile; *nakra* and *kumbhīra* mean alligator. Then, *mahīlatā*, *gaṇḍūpada*, *kiñculaka*, *nihākā*, and *godhikā* are synonyms for the earth-lizard (mole-crawler).
(1.10.560) *Gaṇḍūpada*, *kiñculaka*, *nihākā*, and *godhikā* are the same.
*Raktapā* refers to the leech in the feminine; *jalaukasaḥ* is used in the plural.

*Muktāsphoṭa* and *śukti* denote the pearl-oyster shell in the feminine. *Śaṅkha* and *kambu* refer to the conch shell and are used in the masculine and neuter genders. *Kṣudraśaṅkhāḥ*, *śaṅkhanakhāḥ*, *śambūkāḥ*, and *jalaśuktayaḥ* all refer to small shells.
(1.10.564) Bheka, maṇḍūka, varṣābhū, śālūra, plava, and dardura are synonyms for a frog.
(1.10.565) Śilī and gaṇḍūpadī refer to a female earthworm; varṣābhvī is a female frog; kamaṭhī and ḍuli refer to a female tortoise.
(1.10.566) Śṛṅgī is the mate of the madgura fish; durnāmā and dīrghakośikā refer to the leech.
(1.10.567) Reservoirs and water-holders; among these, a *hrada* is a lake with unfathomable water. (1.10.568) An *āhāva* or *nipāna* is a watering place near a well or a reservoir.
(1.10.569) *Andhu*, *prahi*, and *kūpa* are masculine terms for a well; whereas *udapāna* may be used in the masculine.
The rim of a well is its *vīnāha*; that which serves as its mouth-binding is the *mukhabandhana*.
A dug-out pond is a *puṣkariṇī*, while a natural pool is an *akhāta* or *devakhātaka*. A lotus-pond is a *taḍāga* (not feminine), *kāsāra*, *sarasī*, or *saras*.
(1.10.573) A *veśanta* is a pool or a small lake; a *vāpī* is a long pond. (1.10.574) A *kheya* is a ditch, while an *ādhāra* is that wherein the holding of waters occurs.
(1.10.575) An *ālavāla*, *āvāla*, or *āvāpa* is a water-trough for trees; furthermore, a *nadī* is a river.
Taraṅgiṇī, śaivalinī, taṭinī, hrādinī, dhunī, srotasvinī,
dvīpavatī, sravantī, nimnagā, apagā,
kūlaṅkaṣā, nirjhariṇī, rodhovakrā, and sarasvatī.
The Gaṅgā is called Viṣṇupadī, Jahnutanayā, Suranimnagā, Bhāgīrathī, Tripathagā, Trisrotā, and also the mother of Bhīṣma.
The Kālindī is called Sūryatanayā, Yamunā, and Śamanasvasā.
The Revā is the Narmadā, the Somodbhavā, and the Mekalakanyakā;
the Karatoyā is the Sadānīrā; the Bāhudā is the Saitavāhinī;
the Śatadrū is the Śutudri; and the Vipāśā is the Vipāṭ in the feminine.
The Śoṇa is the Hiraṇyavāha; a small artificial river is called a *kulyā*.
The Śarāvatī, Vetravatī, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, and other rivers are also [named]. The confluence of rivers is called a *sambheda* or a *saṅgama*.
The two channels for water are called *praṇālī*; the latter two [terms] apply to three [types of water].
In the Devikā and Sarayū rivers, the words *dāvika* and *sārava* are used respectively. *Saugandhika*, however, is the *kalhāra*; *hallaka* is the red *sandhyaka*.
The *utpala*, *kuvalaya*, *nīlāmbujanman*, and *indīvara* are synonyms for the blue lotus; whereas *kumuda* and *kairava* refer to the white lotus.
The root (*kanda*) of these is called *śālūka*. The *vāriparṇī* is the *kumbhikā*.
*Jalanīlī*, *śaivāla*, and *śaivala* denote moss. *Kumudvatī*, *kumudinī*, *nalinī*, *visinī*, *padminī*, and so forth, denote the night-lotus plant;
alternatively, these words may also be masculine, as in *padma*, *nalina*, *aravinda*, and *mahotpala*.

The thousand-petaled lotus, the hundred-petaled lotus, the water-born, the mud-born, the crimson, the excellent, the lake-born, the lotus born from the stalk, the royal lotus, the flower, the water-lily, and the ambhoruha.

(1.10.600) *Puṇḍarīka* is a white lotus; furthermore, for a red lotus, (1.10.601) *raktotpala* and *kokanada* [are used]. *Nāla* and *nāla* [mean] the stalk, and it is not feminine. (1.10.602) *Mṛṇāla* and *bisa* [refer to the lotus fiber]; for a cluster of lotuses and the like, *khaṇḍa* is used and is not feminine.

*karahāṭa* is the root-stalk; *kiñjalka* and *kesara* (masculine/neuter) denote the filament; *saṃvartikā* and *navadala* refer to the new leaf; *bījakośa* and *varāṭaka* denote the seed-vessel; and *kāṇḍasamāpti* refers to the end of the stalk.
(1.11.605) Heaven, the sky, the directions, time, intellect, sound, and so forth, along with drama; (1.11.606) the netherworld, the serpent-dwellers, hell, and water, as well as their combinations—
thus [ends] the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* composed by Amarasiṃha.
